beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.
beats.got: The agents coordinate through shared files. That is a bit less slogan-like than I expected.

beats.trigger: Schedule your personal agent to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** when splitting pays off and when one agent wins
beats.got: A list of verbs like every programme has. The last item says one agent can win, which is unusual.

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: Six agents on our own documents. Fine, I'll see whether it works.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Slack changes another system.
beats.got: Someone has thought about what the agent may and may not touch. It writes the message first and sends only after approval.

beats.trigger: Push back when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: The agent reads my earlier notes and tries to name the one thing that matters. It admits the first answer will probably be weak, which I trust more.

beats.trigger: If an agent starts reading the world, stop it, steer narrower, then say *"continue"*.
beats.got: Three searches run in parallel on our own wiki, docs and the web. I can see them and steer them, so I can test this myself.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if the answer is right. That is expected. Name the doubt; don't fix it here.
beats.got: The course says up front that I cannot yet verify the result. Nobody has said that to me in a training before.

beats.trigger: When do you split, and how?
beats.got: A question about when not to use several agents.

beats.trigger: A hundred tiny agents cost more to coordinate than they save.
beats.got: One agent per recurring job. It sounds like process design, which I know.

beats.trigger: Default to one agent with a good prompt.
beats.got: The training starts with 'don't'. I did not expect a vendor-ish course to say that.

beats.trigger: A backward planner and a reframer in the same voice are one agent pretending to be two.
beats.got: Three clear tests for splitting: access, dialect, stance. Access is the same logic as separation of duties.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.
beats.got: More agents does not mean more rigour. That is the honest limit I was waiting for.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Without a framework the synthesis is an even average. A framework forces a choice, though it is Rumelt again and I am not sure it is right.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: A test I can apply to any proposal, including a vendor's.

beats.trigger: Each helper gets one job, reports back as a file and disappears.
beats.got: Separate sessions for long-lived agents, helpers for short jobs.

beats.trigger: One agent can call another for a different stance, source zone, or working style.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.
beats.got: The failures happen at the handoffs, and the example is concrete. I have seen the same thing between human teams.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.
beats.got: This repeats an earlier slide.

beats.trigger: confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: The module lists failure modes openly.

beats.trigger: Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.
beats.got: You ask the agent to diagnose itself. I want to see what it actually finds.

beats.trigger: add a rule to CLAUDE.md: what to read first, what not to smooth over
beats.got: A sensible debugging checklist. Write the lesson down so it is not lost.

beats.trigger: then rewrites CLAUDE.md in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites its own rules. Interesting, but I would want to read the diff.

beats.trigger: It does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: The audit checks the handoffs, not whether the result is true. They say so themselves.

beats.trigger: *"The Confluence retriever kept normalising before writing."*
beats.got: I argue with the summary and the agent adjusts. That's fine.

beats.trigger: The synthesized briefing's correctness stays an open question today.
beats.got: The course tells me the output may be wrong and does not pretend otherwise. That is why I would consider continuing.

beats.trigger: New evidence tests the memory's structure.
beats.got: Optional homework. Probably skipped.

beats.trigger: Split only where agents can't be one: access, dialect, stance.
beats.got: Two lines I can remember: split by access, dialect or stance, otherwise use one agent.

beats.trigger: Pre-reads before Module 4
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Agent risk sits on top of normal security.
beats.got: Agents add prompt injection and non-deterministic behaviour on top of normal security. The GDPR question is coming.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: An agent has the same access as whoever connected it, and nobody had mentioned that until now.

beats.trigger: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Use one agent by default and split only for different access, dialect or stance. That works as a test on any vendor pitch.
The handoffs between agents are where it fails, and the synthesized answer is not checked for truth. I need to verify it myself.
Running several searches in parallel over our own wiki and documents is something that was not practical two years ago.

monday.move: Nothing on Monday. Maybe later, one retriever run on a real question from our partner strategy, and I would check the output against what I already know.
monday.when: Not before the programme's steering groups ease off, maybe in two weeks
monday.stop_condition: If the output tells me nothing I did not already know, or if I cannot trace the claims to sources
monday.blocker: My calendar, and my doubt about whether the output is reliable enough to act on

misconception.why: The course said 'don't' and named its own limits, which the earlier programmes never did. The parallel searches on our own documents also did something I could see. I still think much of the hype will blow over, but I no longer think I can just wait.

one_line: Less of a sales pitch than I expected. It told me when not to use it and that the answer might be wrong. I'll try it once on a real question.
